15:Tb6de,<p>React has four names that beginners treat as interchangeable: <code>ReactNode</code>, <code>ReactElement</code>, <code>Component</code>, and plain tag names like <code>div</code>. They look like they mean roughly the same thing. They don't. Sorting them out clarifies what lives in JS memory, what lands in the DOM, and what gets called when.</p>
<h2>Four kinds, one sentence each</h2>






























<table><thead><tr><th>Name</th><th>What it is</th><th>Real or logical</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><strong>ReactNode</strong></td><td>A TypeScript type. The widest bucket: anything React can render.</td><td>Logical</td></tr><tr><td><strong>ReactElement</strong></td><td>A plain JS object produced by JSX or <code>createElement</code>. Shape: <code>{ type, props, key, ref }</code>.</td><td>Logical</td></tr><tr><td><strong>Component</strong></td><td>A function or class. Takes props, returns elements.</td><td>Logical (it's code)</td></tr><tr><td><strong><code>div</code></strong></td><td>A string. An HTML tag name.</td><td>Logical as a string. Becomes a real <code>HTMLDivElement</code> after commit.</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p>Everything except the final DOM output lives in JS memory. Only the DOM node that React commits into the browser is real.</p>
<h2>How they stack</h2>
<p>The four are not on the same axis. Some are hierarchical, some are peer, one is a producer of another.</p>
<p><strong>ReactNode ⊃ ReactElement.</strong> ReactNode is the widest type. It includes everything React will render: <code>ReactElement</code>, strings, numbers, null, undefined, false, arrays of ReactNodes, Fragments. ReactElement is just one kind.</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="ts" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="ts" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// All of these are ReactNode. Only the first is ReactElement.</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">&#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">div </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">/></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">             // ReactElement</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'hello'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">             // string</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">42</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">                  // number</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">[</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">&#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">a</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">/></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">, &#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">b</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">/>]        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// array</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">&#x3C;>...&#x3C;/></span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">            // Fragment</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p><strong>Component and <code>'div'</code> are peers.</strong> Look at the shape of a ReactElement:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="ts" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="ts" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{ type, props, key, ref }</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>The <code>type</code> field can be either a string like <code>'div'</code> (a host component) or a Component (a function or class). Same slot, two valid inhabitants. Neither is a subcategory of the other.</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">&#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#85E89D;--shiki-light:#22863A">div</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>hi&#x3C;/</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#85E89D;--shiki-light:#22863A">div</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>        </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// type: 'div'      (string, host)</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">&#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">Button</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>hi&#x3C;/</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">Button</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>  </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// type: Button     (function, user)</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>React inspects <code>type</code> during reconciliation:</p>
<ul>
<li>String type: prepare a real DOM node at commit.</li>
<li>Function or class: call it, expand into more elements.</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Component produces ReactElements.</strong> A component is a function. You call it (or write <code>&#x3C;Name /></code>) and it returns one or more ReactElements. The component itself never appears on screen. What appears are the elements it produces.</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">function</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> Button</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">({ </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#FFAB70;--shiki-light:#E36209">label</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> }) {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">  return</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> &#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#85E89D;--shiki-light:#22863A">span</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>{label}&#x3C;/</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#85E89D;--shiki-light:#22863A">span</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>   </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// returns a ReactElement</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<h2>Chasing one button from Component to HTMLElement</h2>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="jsx" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">function</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> Greeting</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">({ </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#FFAB70;--shiki-light:#E36209">name</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> }) {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">  return</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> &#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#85E89D;--shiki-light:#22863A">div</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">>Hello, {name}&#x3C;/</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#85E89D;--shiki-light:#22863A">div</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">></span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span>
<span data-line=""> </span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">const</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> tree</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49"> =</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> &#x3C;</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">Greeting</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> name</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">"Jialin"</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> /></span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p><code>tree</code> is a ReactElement. Its <code>type</code> field is the <code>Greeting</code> function itself:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  type</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: Greeting,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  props</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: { </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">name</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'Jialin'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> },</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  key</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  ref</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>React walks in and sees <code>type: Greeting</code>. It's a function, so React calls it with the props:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// After Greeting({ name: 'Jialin' }) runs:</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  type</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'div'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  props</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: { </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">children</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: [</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'Hello, '</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">, </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'Jialin'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">] },</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  key</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  ref</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Now <code>type</code> is the string <code>'div'</code>. React knows this is a host component. It wraps this element in a <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js"><strong>Fiber</strong></a> node, which holds all the bookkeeping React needs:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">{</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  type</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'div'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,                    </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// same as the element</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  stateNode</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,                </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// will hold HTMLDivElement after commit</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  child</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,                    </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// first child Fiber</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">  sibling</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,                  </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// next sibling</span></span>

<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>A ReactElement is a throwaway snapshot of what the UI should look like. A Fiber is React's persistent work record. Elements get discarded after each render; Fibers live on (in fact two trees of them: <code>current</code> and <code>workInProgress</code>, swapped at commit).</p>
<p>In <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js">commit phase</a>, React reads the Fiber's <code>flags</code> and calls the matching DOM operation: <code>document.createElement('div')</code>, <code>insertBefore</code>, <code>setAttribute</code>, and so on. That's when <code>stateNode</code> gets populated with the actual <code>HTMLDivElement</code> and the node joins the real DOM.</p>
<p>The full chain:</p>
<pre><code>Component Greeting                              source code, always present
   ↓ called
ReactElement { type: Greeting }                 throwaway, discarded after this render
   ↓ Greeting runs, returns
ReactElement { type: 'div' }                    throwaway, discarded after this render
   ↓ React reconciles
Fiber { type: 'div', stateNode, child, ... }   persistent, lives across renders
   ↓ commit phase
HTMLDivElement                                  real, in the browser's DOM
</code></pre>
<h2>The two trees, and the swap</h2>
<p>React keeps two fiber trees: <code>current</code> (on screen) and <code>workInProgress</code> (being built). Here's the puzzle: both trees' fibers <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js">point their <code>stateNode</code> at the same <code>HTMLDivElement</code></a> (search <code>createWorkInProgress</code>, which copies <code>stateNode</code> from current to wip). So shouldn't rebuilding workInProgress leak into the DOM?</p>
<p>No, because a pointer is a read channel, not a write channel. Writing to the DOM needs explicit calls like <code>setAttribute</code>, <code>appendChild</code>, <code>removeChild</code>, which React only makes during <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js">commit's mutation stage</a> (search <code>commitMutationEffectsOnFiber</code>). Rebuilding workInProgress only touches the fiber's own fields:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">wipFiber.memoizedProps </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> { children: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#9ECBFF;--shiki-light:#032F62">'new text'</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> }  </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// Fiber's own field</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">wipFiber.flags </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">|=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> Update                           </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// Fiber's own field</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">wipFiber.child </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> newChildFiber                     </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// Fiber's own tree pointer</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>Think of <code>stateNode</code> as a TV remote, and the DOM as the TV. Both <code>current</code> and <code>workInProgress</code> hold the same remote. You can examine it, flip it around, hand it back and forth. The TV does not react. Only when someone presses a button (commit's mutation stage) does the channel change.</p>
<p>So why keep two fibers at all? For a node that didn't change, why not point workInProgress straight at current and save the copy? Because the fiber is scratch space React writes the next version onto. If workInProgress <em>were</em> the current fiber, those writes would land on the tree that's on screen. Two fibers give React a private draft to mutate, discard, and rebuild while the live tree stays untouched.</p>
<p>They link through <code>alternate</code>. <code>current.alternate</code> points to its twin, and back. Two addresses, and they take turns:</p>
<pre><code>Render 1:  current = A,  workInProgress = B
  commit → current moves to B
Render 2:  current = B,  workInProgress = A   (A reset and reused)
Render 3:  current = A,  workInProgress = B
</code></pre>
<p>"The fiber for this component" is not a stable object. It ping-pongs between A and B every render. What's stable is the pair, and the <code>stateNode</code> both of them point at. Two cheap bookkeeping objects, recycled; one real DOM node, shared.</p>
<p>The mechanism is <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js"><code>createWorkInProgress</code></a>, trimmed to the parts that matter:</p>

<p>No twin yet? Allocate one, point its <code>stateNode</code> at the <em>same</em> DOM node, wire <code>alternate</code> both ways. Twin exists? Reuse it, zero its flags. That <code>else</code> branch is the recycling: two objects, reused forever, never a third.</p>
<h3>What commit actually swaps</h3>
<p>Two things happen at commit. Only one is visible.</p>
<pre><code>mutation → change the real DOM (setAttribute, appendChild, removeChild)   ← user sees this
swap     → root.current = workInProgress                                  ← internal only
layout   → useLayoutEffect, componentDidMount
</code></pre>
<p>The DOM is mutated in place: same nodes, changed attributes, a few added or removed. By the time the swap runs, the DOM is already updated, so flipping <code>current</code> repaints nothing. React swaps only so the <em>next</em> render has the right baseline and the A/B recycling works. Mutation faces the user; the swap is React talking to itself.</p>
<p>The swap is one line in <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js"><code>commitRoot</code></a>:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">root.current </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> finishedWork;</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">pendingEffectsStatus </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> PENDING_LAYOUT_PHASE</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">;</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p><code>finishedWork</code> is the workInProgress tree. The line sits after the mutation phase (DOM already updated) and right before the layout phase, which is why <code>useLayoutEffect</code> and <code>componentDidMount</code> read the new tree as <code>current</code>.</p>
<h3>Mount, update, delete</h3>
<p>The <code>alternate</code> story has three cases, and only one is <code>null</code>:</p>
<pre><code>mount   in wip, not in current   →  wip fiber's alternate = null   (the real "points to null")
update  in both                  →  two fibers, alternate ↔ alternate, reused
delete  in current, not in wip    →  no wip fiber is built for it
</code></pre>
<p>Deletion is the one people guess wrong. React doesn't null an alternate to mean "gone." The removed node just gets no workInProgress fiber; React pushes the old one onto its parent's <code>deletions</code> list and flags the parent <code>ChildDeletion</code>. Commit reads that list and calls <code>removeChild</code>. After the swap, nothing points at the orphan, so it's collected.</p>
<p>The code is <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js"><code>deleteChild</code></a>:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">function</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1"> deleteChild</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#FFAB70;--shiki-light:#E36209">returnFiber</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">, </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#FFAB70;--shiki-light:#E36209">childToDelete</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">) {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">  const</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> deletions</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49"> =</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> returnFiber.deletions;</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">  if</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> (deletions </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">===</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5"> null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">) {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    returnFiber.deletions </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> [childToDelete];  </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// parent keeps a deletion list</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    returnFiber.flags </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">|=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> ChildDeletion;       </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// and gets flagged</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  } </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">else</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">    deletions.</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">push</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">(childToDelete);</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  }</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">}</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p><code>returnFiber</code> is the parent. The removed child is pushed onto the parent's <code>deletions</code> array and the parent gets a <code>ChildDeletion</code> flag. Nothing touches an <code>alternate</code>. Deletion is a note on the parent, not a null on the child.</p>
<p>This whole two-tree scheme is what makes Concurrent mode possible. React builds workInProgress, throws it away, restarts, builds again, none of it visible, because the DOM stays untouched until commit.</p>
<h2>Where useState actually lives</h2>
<p>The Fiber sketch had one line worth expanding:</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#B392F0;--shiki-light:#6F42C1">memoizedState</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,   </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#6A737D;--shiki-light:#6A737D">// for function components, this is the hooks chain</span></span></code></pre></figure>
<p>A function component is just a function. It runs, returns, and its locals vanish. So where does <code>useState</code> keep its value between renders? Not in the function. A local <code>let</code> resets every call.</p>
<p>It lives on the Fiber, in <code>memoizedState</code>, as a linked list of hooks. Each <code>useState</code>, <code>useRef</code>, <code>useEffect</code> is one node:</p>
<pre><code>Fiber.memoizedState → hook1 → hook2 → hook3 → ...
                      useState useRef useEffect
</code></pre>
<p>The Fiber persists across renders (that's the whole "persistent, not throwaway" point), so state parked on it survives. Each render React calls your function; when you hit <code>useState</code>, it walks to the next hook node and hands back what's stored.</p>
<p>"The next node" is the catch. React does not know your variable names. It cannot see that one <code>useState</code> is <code>name</code> and another is <code>age</code>. It only counts: the first hook call gets the first node, the second call gets the second, and so on. Position is the only thing tying a value back to you.</p>
<p>Not a metaphor. Here is the hook node React allocates, straight from <a href="https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberHooks.js">its source</a> (search <code>mountWorkInProgressHook</code>):</p>
<figure data-rehype-pretty-code-figure=""><pre tabindex="0" data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light"><code data-language="js" data-theme="github-dark github-light" style="display: grid;"><span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">var</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> hook </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#F97583;--shiki-light:#D73A49">=</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E"> {</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  memoizedState: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  baseState: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>
<span data-line=""><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">  baseQueue: </span><span style="--shiki-dark:#79B8FF;--shiki-light:#005CC5">null</span><span style="--shiki-dark:#E1E4E8;--shiki-light:#24292E">,</span></span>

<p><strong>Why can't you return a Component from another component?</strong></p>
<p>What you return is supposed to be a ReactNode. A Component is a function; the function reference is not a renderable node. You need to render it: <code>&#x3C;Comp /></code>, not just <code>Comp</code>.</p>

It might be a component, or a render prop you meant to call yourself: <code>&#x3C;Provider>{data => &#x3C;div />}&#x3C;/Provider></code>. Auto-rendering every function would break that pattern. Making you write <code>&#x3C;Comp /></code> keeps the intent explicit.</p>
<p><strong>Why is <code>null</code> fine to return but a function not?</strong></p>
<p><code>null</code> is a valid ReactNode (meaning "render nothing here"). A function reference is not. ReactNode's union type allows nullish values, primitives, elements, and arrays. It does not allow arbitrary functions.</p>
<p><strong>Why does changing a list item's <code>key</code> reset its state?</strong></p>
<p>During reconciliation React matches new elements to existing Fibers by <code>key</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Same key and type</strong>: reuse the Fiber, keep its <code>memoizedState</code> and its DOM node.</li>
<li><strong>Different key</strong>: discard the old Fiber, build a new one with empty state.</li>
</ul>
<p>So <code>key</code> is a Fiber's identity across renders. It's also why an array index makes a shaky key. Insert a row at the top and every index shifts, so React reuses the wrong Fiber for the wrong row, and state sticks to the wrong item.</p>
<h2>The punchline</h2>
<p>The React tree in JS memory is all <strong>ReactElements</strong>.<br>
Each element's <code>type</code> is a string (becomes a DOM node) or a Component (gets called, produces more elements).<br>
React finds the tree by recursion.<br>
Reconciliation flattens it into Fibers.<br>
Only after commit do the string-typed elements become real DOM.</p>
<p>Four names, three kinds of value, one real output.</p>

<p>Related: <a href="/v2/from-setstate-to-pixels">from setState to pixels</a> and <a href="/v2/inside-react-fiberworkloop">Inside React's FiberWorkLoop</a>.</p>16:T41e8,
React has four names that beginners treat as interchangeable: `ReactNode`, `ReactElement`, `Component`, and plain tag names like `div`. They look like they mean roughly the same thing. They don't. Sorting them out clarifies what lives in JS memory, what lands in the DOM, and what gets called when.

## Four kinds, one sentence each

| Name | What it is | Real or logical |
|---|---|---|
| **ReactNode** | A TypeScript type. The widest bucket: anything React can render. | Logical |
| **ReactElement** | A plain JS object produced by JSX or `createElement`. Shape: `{ type, props, key, ref }`. | Logical |
| **Component** | A function or class. Takes props, returns elements. | Logical (it's code) |
| **`div`** | A string. An HTML tag name. | Logical as a string. Becomes a real `HTMLDivElement` after commit. |

Everything except the final DOM output lives in JS memory. Only the DOM node that React commits into the browser is real.

## How they stack

The four are not on the same axis. Some are hierarchical, some are peer, one is a producer of another.

**ReactNode ⊃ ReactElement.** ReactNode is the widest type. It includes everything React will render: `ReactElement`, strings, numbers, null, undefined, false, arrays of ReactNodes, Fragments. ReactElement is just one kind.

```ts
// All of these are ReactNode. Only the first is ReactElement.
<div />             // ReactElement
'hello'             // string
42                  // number
null
[<a/>, <b/>]        // array
<>...</>            // Fragment
```

**Component and `'div'` are peers.** Look at the shape of a ReactElement:

```ts
{ type, props, key, ref }
```

The `type` field can be either a string like `'div'` (a host component) or a Component (a function or class). Same slot, two valid inhabitants. Neither is a subcategory of the other.

```jsx
<div>hi</div>        // type: 'div'      (string, host)
<Button>hi</Button>  // type: Button     (function, user)
```

React inspects `type` during reconciliation:

- String type: prepare a real DOM node at commit.
- Function or class: call it, expand into more elements.

**Component produces ReactElements.** A component is a function. You call it (or write `<Name />`) and it returns one or more ReactElements. The component itself never appears on screen. What appears are the elements it produces.

```jsx
function Button({ label }) {
  return <span>{label}</span>   // returns a ReactElement
}
```

## Chasing one button from Component to HTMLElement

```jsx
function Greeting({ name }) {
  return <div>Hello, {name}</div>
}

const tree = <Greeting name="Jialin" />
```

`tree` is a ReactElement. Its `type` field is the `Greeting` function itself:

```js
{
  type: Greeting,
  props: { name: 'Jialin' },
  key: null,
  ref: null
}
```

React walks in and sees `type: Greeting`. It's a function, so React calls it with the props:

```js
// After Greeting({ name: 'Jialin' }) runs:
{
  type: 'div',
  props: { children: ['Hello, ', 'Jialin'] },
  key: null,
  ref: null
}
```

Now `type` is the string `'div'`. React knows this is a host component. It wraps this element in a [**Fiber**](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js) node, which holds all the bookkeeping React needs:

```js
{
  type: 'div',                    // same as the element
  stateNode: null,                // will hold HTMLDivElement after commit
  child: null,                    // first child Fiber
  sibling: null,                  // next sibling
  return: ParentFiber,            // parent (named 'return' for historical reasons)
  alternate: Fiber,               // the other tree in double buffering
  memoizedProps: { children: ['Hello, ', 'Jialin'] },
  memoizedState: null,            // for function components, this is the hooks chain
  lanes: /* bitmask */,           // priority for Scheduler
  flags: /* bitmask */,           // Placement, Update, Deletion, etc.
}
```

A ReactElement is a throwaway snapshot of what the UI should look like. A Fiber is React's persistent work record. Elements get discarded after each render; Fibers live on (in fact two trees of them: `current` and `workInProgress`, swapped at commit).

In [commit phase](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js), React reads the Fiber's `flags` and calls the matching DOM operation: `document.createElement('div')`, `insertBefore`, `setAttribute`, and so on. That's when `stateNode` gets populated with the actual `HTMLDivElement` and the node joins the real DOM.

The full chain:

```
Component Greeting                              source code, always present
   ↓ called
ReactElement { type: Greeting }                 throwaway, discarded after this render
   ↓ Greeting runs, returns
ReactElement { type: 'div' }                    throwaway, discarded after this render
   ↓ React reconciles
Fiber { type: 'div', stateNode, child, ... }   persistent, lives across renders
   ↓ commit phase
HTMLDivElement                                  real, in the browser's DOM
```

## The two trees, and the swap

React keeps two fiber trees: `current` (on screen) and `workInProgress` (being built). Here's the puzzle: both trees' fibers [point their `stateNode` at the same `HTMLDivElement`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js) (search `createWorkInProgress`, which copies `stateNode` from current to wip). So shouldn't rebuilding workInProgress leak into the DOM?

No, because a pointer is a read channel, not a write channel. Writing to the DOM needs explicit calls like `setAttribute`, `appendChild`, `removeChild`, which React only makes during [commit's mutation stage](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberCommitWork.js) (search `commitMutationEffectsOnFiber`). Rebuilding workInProgress only touches the fiber's own fields:

```js
wipFiber.memoizedProps = { children: 'new text' }  // Fiber's own field
wipFiber.flags |= Update                           // Fiber's own field
wipFiber.child = newChildFiber                     // Fiber's own tree pointer
```

Think of `stateNode` as a TV remote, and the DOM as the TV. Both `current` and `workInProgress` hold the same remote. You can examine it, flip it around, hand it back and forth. The TV does not react. Only when someone presses a button (commit's mutation stage) does the channel change.

So why keep two fibers at all? For a node that didn't change, why not point workInProgress straight at current and save the copy? Because the fiber is scratch space React writes the next version onto. If workInProgress *were* the current fiber, those writes would land on the tree that's on screen. Two fibers give React a private draft to mutate, discard, and rebuild while the live tree stays untouched.

They link through `alternate`. `current.alternate` points to its twin, and back. Two addresses, and they take turns:

```
Render 1:  current = A,  workInProgress = B
  commit → current moves to B
Render 2:  current = B,  workInProgress = A   (A reset and reused)
Render 3:  current = A,  workInProgress = B
```

"The fiber for this component" is not a stable object. It ping-pongs between A and B every render. What's stable is the pair, and the `stateNode` both of them point at. Two cheap bookkeeping objects, recycled; one real DOM node, shared.

The mechanism is [`createWorkInProgress`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiber.js), trimmed to the parts that matter:

```js
function createWorkInProgress(current, pendingProps) {
  let workInProgress = current.alternate;
  if (workInProgress === null) {
    // no twin yet: allocate one, share the DOM node, wire both directions
    workInProgress = createFiber(current.tag, pendingProps, current.key, current.mode);
    workInProgress.stateNode = current.stateNode;   // same real DOM node
    workInProgress.alternate = current;
    current.alternate = workInProgress;
  } else {
    // twin exists: reuse it, reset its flags
    workInProgress.pendingProps = pendingProps;
    workInProgress.flags = 0;
  }
  workInProgress.child = current.child;
  return workInProgress;
}
```

No twin yet? Allocate one, point its `stateNode` at the *same* DOM node, wire `alternate` both ways. Twin exists? Reuse it, zero its flags. That `else` branch is the recycling: two objects, reused forever, never a third.

### What commit actually swaps

Two things happen at commit. Only one is visible.

```
mutation → change the real DOM (setAttribute, appendChild, removeChild)   ← user sees this
swap     → root.current = workInProgress                                  ← internal only
layout   → useLayoutEffect, componentDidMount
```

The DOM is mutated in place: same nodes, changed attributes, a few added or removed. By the time the swap runs, the DOM is already updated, so flipping `current` repaints nothing. React swaps only so the *next* render has the right baseline and the A/B recycling works. Mutation faces the user; the swap is React talking to itself.

The swap is one line in [`commitRoot`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js):

```js
root.current = finishedWork;
pendingEffectsStatus = PENDING_LAYOUT_PHASE;
```

`finishedWork` is the workInProgress tree. The line sits after the mutation phase (DOM already updated) and right before the layout phase, which is why `useLayoutEffect` and `componentDidMount` read the new tree as `current`.

### Mount, update, delete

The `alternate` story has three cases, and only one is `null`:

```
mount   in wip, not in current   →  wip fiber's alternate = null   (the real "points to null")
update  in both                  →  two fibers, alternate ↔ alternate, reused
delete  in current, not in wip    →  no wip fiber is built for it
```

Deletion is the one people guess wrong. React doesn't null an alternate to mean "gone." The removed node just gets no workInProgress fiber; React pushes the old one onto its parent's `deletions` list and flags the parent `ChildDeletion`. Commit reads that list and calls `removeChild`. After the swap, nothing points at the orphan, so it's collected.

The code is [`deleteChild`](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactChildFiber.js):

```js
function deleteChild(returnFiber, childToDelete) {
  const deletions = returnFiber.deletions;
  if (deletions === null) {
    returnFiber.deletions = [childToDelete];  // parent keeps a deletion list
    returnFiber.flags |= ChildDeletion;       // and gets flagged
  } else {
    deletions.push(childToDelete);
  }
}
```

`returnFiber` is the parent. The removed child is pushed onto the parent's `deletions` array and the parent gets a `ChildDeletion` flag. Nothing touches an `alternate`. Deletion is a note on the parent, not a null on the child.

This whole two-tree scheme is what makes Concurrent mode possible. React builds workInProgress, throws it away, restarts, builds again, none of it visible, because the DOM stays untouched until commit.

## Where useState actually lives

The Fiber sketch had one line worth expanding:

```js
memoizedState: null,   // for function components, this is the hooks chain
```

A function component is just a function. It runs, returns, and its locals vanish. So where does `useState` keep its value between renders? Not in the function. A local `let` resets every call.

It lives on the Fiber, in `memoizedState`, as a linked list of hooks. Each `useState`, `useRef`, `useEffect` is one node:

```
Fiber.memoizedState → hook1 → hook2 → hook3 → ...
                      useState useRef useEffect
```

The Fiber persists across renders (that's the whole "persistent, not throwaway" point), so state parked on it survives. Each render React calls your function; when you hit `useState`, it walks to the next hook node and hands back what's stored.

"The next node" is the catch. React does not know your variable names. It cannot see that one `useState` is `name` and another is `age`. It only counts: the first hook call gets the first node, the second call gets the second, and so on. Position is the only thing tying a value back to you.

Not a metaphor. Here is the hook node React allocates, straight from [its source](https://github.com/facebook/react/blob/main/packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberHooks.js) (search `mountWorkInProgressHook`):

```js
var hook = {
  memoizedState: null,
  baseState: null,
  baseQueue: null,
  queue: null,
  next: null,
}
```

No name, no key, no id. The only link from one hook to the next is `next`. React could not match by name if it wanted to. Position is all it has.

So the order has to be identical every render. Watch what breaks when a hook hides inside an `if`:

```jsx
function Profile({ show }) {
  if (show) {
    const [name] = useState('Ann')   // sometimes called, sometimes skipped
  }
  const [age] = useState(20)
}
```

First render, `show` is true. Two calls, two nodes:

```
call 1 → node 1 = 'Ann'   (name)
call 2 → node 2 = 20      (age)
```

Next render, `show` is false. The `if` skips the first call. One call is left, and React still counts from the top:

```
call 1 (age) → node 1 = 'Ann'   // age reads name's value. Wrong.
```

`age` lands on the first node and gets `'Ann'`. Every hook after the skipped one shifts up a slot and reads the wrong value. React also expected two hooks and saw one, so it throws. That is the whole reason hooks stay at the top level: never inside `if`, `for`, or after an early return.

It also closes the loop with `key`. Change a component's key and React builds a new Fiber, with a fresh empty `memoizedState`. That's why a changed key resets state: no special rule, just a different Fiber.

## Some confusions cleared

**Why does `<MyComponent />` render but `<myComponent />` (lowercase) not?**

JSX uses capitalization to decide: uppercase means `type` is a Component reference; lowercase means `type` is a string host name. Lowercase with an undefined reference silently becomes a DOM attempt for `<mycomponent>`, which browsers ignore.

Compile it and the branch is right there in the output:

```js
<div />          →  createElement("div", ...)          // lowercase: a string
<MyComponent />  →  createElement(MyComponent, ...)    // uppercase: a variable
<myComponent />  →  createElement("myComponent", ...)  // lowercase, still a string
```

That last line is the trap. `<myComponent />` looks like a component, but the lowercase first letter makes the compiler emit the string `"myComponent"`. React gets `type: "myComponent"`, treats it as an unknown host tag, and the browser drops `<mycomponent>`. Worth noting: this split is [the JSX compiler's rule](https://react.dev/learn/your-first-component), not React's. React only ever sees the `type` the compiler already decided.

**Why can't you return a Component from another component?**

What you return is supposed to be a ReactNode. A Component is a function; the function reference is not a renderable node. You need to render it: `<Comp />`, not just `Comp`.

React could check `typeof === 'function'` and call it for you. It refuses on purpose. A bare function in the tree is ambiguous. It might be a component, or a render prop you meant to call yourself: `<Provider>{data => <div />}</Provider>`. Auto-rendering every function would break that pattern. Making you write `<Comp />` keeps the intent explicit.

**Why is `null` fine to return but a function not?**

`null` is a valid ReactNode (meaning "render nothing here"). A function reference is not. ReactNode's union type allows nullish values, primitives, elements, and arrays. It does not allow arbitrary functions.

**Why does changing a list item's `key` reset its state?**

During reconciliation React matches new elements to existing Fibers by `key`:

- **Same key and type**: reuse the Fiber, keep its `memoizedState` and its DOM node.
- **Different key**: discard the old Fiber, build a new one with empty state.

So `key` is a Fiber's identity across renders. It's also why an array index makes a shaky key. Insert a row at the top and every index shifts, so React reuses the wrong Fiber for the wrong row, and state sticks to the wrong item.

## The punchline

The React tree in JS memory is all **ReactElements**.\
Each element's `type` is a string (becomes a DOM node) or a Component (gets called, produces more elements).\
React finds the tree by recursion.\
Reconciliation flattens it into Fibers.\
Only after commit do the string-typed elements become real DOM.

Four names, three kinds of value, one real output.

---

Related: [from setState to pixels](/v2/from-setstate-to-pixels) and [Inside React's FiberWorkLoop](/v2/inside-react-fiberworkloop).
